Adult females ultimately reach a typical body mass of 29 grams [Wwi = 29 grams], although field surveys have documented considerable variation, with individuals spanning a range from 22 to 36 grams. This size dimorphism likely reflects local resource availability and the energetic costs of lactation, which in this species is a metabolically demanding phase of the reproductive cycle. This rapid onset of sexual maturation, coupled with the short gestation interval of 23 days, enables females to begin reproducing within the same season they were born, contributing to high annual population growth rates. However, the timing of first reproduction is often delayed in harsher environments, where resource limitation restricts juvenile growth. The combination of early maturation, moderate lifespans, and multiple reproductive events per year creates a life history strategy that is highly responsive to fluctuating food availability and habitat quality. In comparison to other *Peromyscus* species, such as the cotton mouse (*Peromyscus gossypinus*), *P. boylii* appears to invest in earlier maturation at the expense of slightly reduced maximum female body mass, a trade-off that reflects its adaptation to more open and arid environments.
